doc.title: Barry Kernfeld interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 16, 2020

title: Sorting out jazz myths by cross-checking sources for Grove
summary: Kernfeld explains checking primary sources and everyone against everyone for Grove, and why accurate relationships matter, citing a woman musician who understated her age.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players

blocks.x: I’m always happy to be timely. And of course there’s no lack of jazz myths about things happen, and this person said that to that person. And I wonder if you can tell me how you sorted out all that, to the best of your ability?
Yeah. And we’re sorting it out all over again as we do the twenty year update to the Second Edition.

Yes, we’re working on that now. I would say that insofar as it’s possible to check primary sources, which now with Ancestry includes a huge wealth of genealogical documents, and family blogs, family trees, things like that. So that helps sort things out. Musicians’ unions reports, so-and-so traveled here, record company catalogues. And what we found doing the Grove because jazz is this small, small world of interlocking relationships. And what we did with Grove that I think no one else had done was to check everybody against everybody else in terms of their relationships, who they played for, who played in their © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

bands, where they played, look at the history of the clubs, look at the band lists, and when it disagreed you might get the same thing nineteen times and find the right one on the twentieth, and that the other nineteen were just copying from each other. We tried to cross check just exhaustively in every source that we could get our hands at, whether it’s a written document, iconography, photographs. So that’s part of your answer. I would like to say, you know, something about why. Because people might think that we’re just fuss pots. You know like who cares if he joined in 1955 or 1956, or in fact he met, they met in 1955 in Berlin and then joined the group in Hamburg in 1956? And to an extent maybe it is fussiness, but I think for one thing jazz is obsessed, perhaps too obsessed, with precedents, with the originals and the copiers, with the innovators and the imitators. And if we’re going to talk about stuff like that, if we’re going to think that it’s as important and maybe too important in my opinion. But if we’re going to think if it’s that important we better know, really, who did what when with whom. And not form a bunch of conclusions based on things that aren’t true or just careless, not so much purposeful fictions but just carelessness gets copied and copied and copied and disseminates through liner notes, through interviews and so forth. That matters. I think relationships matter as far as the facts and getting them right. And I’m sorry it’s been twenty years and I don’t remember who it was but I remember I was working on one of the women in jazz and just couldn’t make any sense of her biography until I realized that she had been putting herself forward as three or four years younger than she actually was, and that’s why she was going, you know, “I can’t remember the details, maybe it was in Buffalo with Al Sears or something like that.” These people were classmates. They went to school together. Well that’s not evident if you think they’re three or four years difference in age. But if they’re the same age and in the same city and they grew up together and they played together, that to me says something that goes way beyond factual fussiness into meaningful how this music was made and how these people learned it.
